Numerous streams were out of their banks and several homes in Wentzville had a couple of feet of water in their basements.

Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  One northbound lane of Highway 141 near the intersection with Clayton Road was closed. Also, several roads in the Maryland Heights, Town and Country, Bel-Ridge, Maplewood, Shrewsbury, and University City areas had over 6 inches of water flowing over them.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees onto Highway N just northwest of Lesterville and onto Highway 49 just east of Lesterville.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Over a foot of water covered the intersection of Interstate 70 and 55 downtown.
Thunderstorm winds blew the roof off of two barns, one barn was blown completely over, and numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees on Highway N near Easley and on Highway A near Hartsburg.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor to moderate roof and siding damage to several homes under construction.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including County Roads 240 and 247, as well as County Road 263 just north of County Road 240.
Lightning struck and killed a woman who was walking across an open field after fishing on one of the lakes at the Rocky Fork Lakes Conservation Area north of Columbia.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor damage in the area including bending a large highway sign to the ground.

Thunderstorm winds caused structural damage to a three story brick building in downtown Quincy.  The entire brick wall on the back of the building blew down and fell onto cars in the parking lot.  No injuries were reported.  Also, a retirement community building had several windows blown out and numerous trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several 200 year old oak trees and caused roof damage to several barns.
Several trees were blown down in Fishhook.
Several trees were blown down in Perry.
Several trees were blown down in Versailles.
Several large tree limbs were blown down.
Several power lines were blown down on Principia College Campus.
Several large tree limbs were blown down in Raymond.
Several large tree limbs and power lines were blown down between Sandoval and Centralia.
Thunderstorm winds damaged a small shed and blew some aluminum siding off of an outbuilding.
Several inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several feet of water was flowing over a couple of roads in the St. Peter area making them impassable.
Thunderstorm winds snapped a power pole in Canton.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree across Highway 11 west of Baring and numerous large tree limbs were blown down in Edina.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous tree limbs and power lines countywide.
Numerous trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down around Quincy.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large oak tree onto Highway E about three quarters of a mile north of Highway 20.
A large tree was blown over onto some power lines in Mexico.
Thunderstorm winds blew over an elm tree.
Thunderstorm winds caused damage to a wall and the roof of a barn.  Also, several power poles were blown down.
Several trees were blown down around town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down large tree limbs in Wellsville and a couple of trees in Middletown.

Thunderstorm winds caused a wide swath of damage extending from Troy to Winfield.  Numerous trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.  In Winfield, winds were estimated around 80 mph.  Several garage doors were caved in and various lawn and play equipment were blown around.  Also, several dozen large trees were blown onto highways, blocking them for a time.

Thunderstorm winds caused a wide swath of tree damage extending from O'Fallon through St. Peters and into St. Charles.  Also, numerous power lines were blown down.  One tree split in half and landed on the front porch of a home causing minor damage.
There was one confirmed death in Madison County during the Heat Wave. A 61 year old Glen Carbon woman was found dead in her mobile home on June 23. The air conditioner in the home was not working.
A 29 year old Griggsville man died of heat stroke while working at a construction site in Valley City.
At least 43 injuries were reported in the City of St. Louis from the excessive heat.

The first Heat Wave of the summer hit from June 17 through June 27. Heat Index values ranged from 100 to 107 during the period. High temperatures ranged from the lower to upper 90s. There were two deaths in St. Louis County from the heat with 80 injuries. 67 people were treated and released at St. Louis County hospitals while 11 were admitted. One death was a 75 year man in Maplewood who was found dead in his home. There were 3 fans running but the air conditioner was not turned on. The other death was a 62 year old woman in Hillsdale who was also found in her home. The windows were shut and there was no air conditioning.

Between 2 and 4 inches of rain with some locally higher amounts fell in a short amount of time over Callaway county.  Several roads were flooded including Highway 94 between Mokane and Steedman and the intersection of Highways 94 and PP just southwest of Mokane.

Between 2 and 4 inches of rain with locally heavier amounts fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Bass Lane and Bonne Femme Church Road just southeast of Columbia, as well as, Blackfoot Road, Crump Lane and Highway KK.
Up to 3 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding in Clinton county.  Numerous roads across the county had water over them.

Between 5 and 6 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding in portions of Hermann.  Frene Creek rose quickly and caused extensive damage to the driveway that leads into the Hermann Middle School parking lot.  Thirty to thirty-five feet of the roadway and bridge were destroyed by the rushing waters.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous large tree limbs in town and along Highway C east of town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several power lines along Highway D.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several 2 to 3 foot diameter trees near Six Flags. Also, a large tree was blown down blocking all west bound lanes of Interstate 44 near mile marker 262.
Several large tree limbs and a power line were blown down in town.

Up to 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  One mile south of Medora, water was flowing over Illinois Route 111.  Also, in Staunton several roads in town were flooded due to the heavy rain.
Several large trees were blown down at the intersection of Highway A and Little Indian Creek Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees, power lines and signs in Salem.

Damaging downburst winds occurred along U.S. Highway 50 in an area from about 2 miles northwest of Iuka to 1 mile northeast of Iuka.  Several trees and tree limbs were blown down.  Also, a machine shed sustained major damage as the south wall was blown down and two other sides buckled in.  The width of this damage swath was approximately 100 yards wide and the wind speeds ranged from 60 to 70 mph.

Another area of downburst winds was surveyed from about 1.5 miles west of Iuka through Iuka to about half a mile east of Iuka.  A large corn field just west of town was flattened by the high winds.  One mobile home was destroyed by a large tree that fell on it.  Numerous large trees and tree limbs were blown down around town.  Some homes sustained minor damage due to the fallen trees and tree limbs.  The width of the damage swath was three quarters of a mile with winds estimated between 70 and 80 mph.
Considerable corn and soybean crop damage due to nickel to quarter size hail that covered the entire ground in some areas.
Several large tree limbs were blown down.
Several trees and power lines were blown down.  Also, one house sustained minor siding damage.
Thunderstorm winds partially flattened a corn field and blew 40 empty train coal cars over. One home in the area sustained moderate roof damage and several power poles were blown over.

Up to 5 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding on numerous roads.  About 6 to 8 inches of water was flowing over Strawberry Road near Allee Road.  Also, Highway C west of High Point was completely covered with water between the north and south branches of Highway CC.  Several streams were flooded south southwest of McGirk.
Thunderstorm winds snapped off tops of a few large trees.  Also, some siding was blown off of a house.

Between 2 and 5 inches of rain has fallen in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Highway 19 both north and south of Interstate 70 had water covering it.  Also, Booneslick Road and Coal Chute Road near High Hill and Sunbeam Road north of New Florence were flooded for a time.
Two to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including a couple of streets in Milton.

Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous trees and tree limbs in town as well as power lines.  A few of the trees caused minor damage to a few homes.  Two vehicles sustained moderate damage from the fallen trees and tree limbs.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous large tree limbs over the southern portions of the county.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees and power lines in town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees including one on Highway W in Stanton, which landed on an unoccupied truck.
Thunderstorm wind blew down several large tree limbs in East Carondelet.
Thunderstorm winds caused moderate roof damage to a mobile home on the east side of town and blew down several large tree limbs in Evansville.
Between 3 and 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Highway 16 east of Monticello, between Sugar Creek and Highway Z.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs onto Highway MM.
Between 2 and 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Highway H had six inches of water over it in spots between U.S. Highway 36 and the south side of Rensselaer.
Up to 6 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Two feet of flowing water covered Highway U east of Lesterville.
Several large tree limbs were blown down.
Thunderstorm winds tore off part of the roof of a business's machine shed about 3 miles southeast of Quincy Regional Airport and threw the debris several hundred feet across Illinois Route 104.
Thunderstorm winds blew part of a machine shed roof off.
Numerous large tree limbs and power lines were blown down throughout town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous large tree limbs and a 30 inch diameter oak tree was snapped off near the base.
Hail fell througout Greenville.
Golfball sized hail was reported on the east side of Greenville at the golf course.

Numerous trees and power lines were blown down through out Greenville.  A two foot diameter tree was snapped off and landed on Illinois Route 140 on the east side of town. Also, one tree fell onto a house causing minor roof damage and another tree fell onto a unoccupied car damaging it.
Several large tree limbs, trees and power lines were blown down.  One tree fell on a house in town causing minor roof damage.

National Weather Service personnel did  a survey of the damage in the Vandalia area and determined that it was straight line wind damage.  Numerous large tree limbs, trees and power lines were blown down.  Overall the damage was produced by 50 to 60 mph winds.  However, there were two areas of damage that suggested slightly higher wind speeds.  One area was a corn field about a mile west of the U.S. Highway 40-Interstate 70 interchange that was completely flattened.  The other area of slightly higher winds was over southern sections of Vandalia.  Tree damage here was a bit more extensive and two large trees were totally uprooted by the winds.  There was also some minor damage to two metal roofs in the area.

A tornado touched down just north of Barrow near Illinois Route 106 and travelled to the northeast crossing County Line Road east of the railroad tracks into Scott County (WFO Lincoln's CWA).  Damage was confined to trees and rated EF0 on the Enhanced Fujita scale.
A tornado touched down about 2.5 miles south southeast of Clayton and travelled to the east.  It only caused damage to trees and tree limbs in the area before crossing into Brown county.

The tornado crossed the Adams/Brown county line about 2.5 miles southwest of Mound Station and continued to travel to the east.  Near the intersection of County roads 1000N and 100E some metal roofing was blown off of a barn, a 3 to 4 foot diameter tree was snapped off near the base, as well as other tree damage.  The tornado soon lifted and dissipated.
Between 2 and 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads and low water crossing were flooded including several streets in Jefferson City.

Between 3 and 5 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time over Franklin county causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including roads near the city park in Union and roads in the Washington area.

High temperatures reached the upper 90's across the St. Louis Metropolitan area. St. Louis County Department of Health reported 7 heat related injuries. Four were treated and released at area hospitals while 3 others had to be admitted.

Very heavy rain fell over central Missouri in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  In Boone county between 4 and 5 inches of rain fell.  Numerous roads were flooded, including Highways E, DD and Y.  Also, several water rescues had to be performed.  There were no injuries or deaths due to the flooding.
Four to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highways 161 and 19 in and around the Montgomery City area.
Three to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including the intersection of Highways Y and EE west of Foley.
Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including County Road 182 and Old Highway 40, as well as several roads in Fulton.
Two to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway N about 2 miles west of Cottleville.
Two to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway F just north of Vandalia.
Two to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded in the Warrenton area including Pinckney Road and Dry Fork Road.

Between 2 and 3 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded countywide, including Highway CC at Tri City Road between Sturgeon and Centralia.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway 151 southeast of Novelty.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway W northeast of Shelbyville.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including County Roads 223 and 221 west of Kingdom City.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Several roads in Paris were flooded.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding. Numerous secondary roads were flooded.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway Y due to water flowing out of Bear Creek.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded and Myers Road, about 5 miles south of Troy, had about 100 yards washed out due to Big Creek overflowing its banks.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway 11 west of Baring and Route F and Highway 151 near Novelty.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including State Route DD near Maud.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including State Route A northeast of Woodlawn.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway BB southeast of Tipton. Also, a car was washed off of Highway BB just south of U.S. 50.  No one was injured due to the incident.

Between 3 and 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway C at the intersection with Silvers Road and Highway N east of the intersection with Highway K.

Between 2 and 3 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were closed including Highway 94 near Mokane and Van Horn Boulevard in Holts Summit.
Between 2 and 3 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Scrivner, Loesch and Bainer Roads.

Between 2 and 3 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including County Road 412 near Loose Creek and County Road 416 near Bonnots Mill.

Between 2 and 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on frozen ground, causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Highway B near Highway 32 in Ste. Genevieve county.  Also, several streets in downtown Ste. Genevieve were covered with several inches of water.

Between 2 and 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time onto frozen ground causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Colony Church and Laws roads on the east side of Farmington.  Also, several roads were flooded in the Desloge area.

Between 2 and 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time onto frozen ground causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Highway O about 8 miles southwest of Fredericktown and Highway V, about 8 miles southeast of Fredericktown.  Also, North Main Street in Fredericktown was closed due to flooding.
Brief period of quarter sized hail with intermixed smaller hail fell at Meramec State Park.
Sixty nine mile per hour wind gust recorded at a University of Missouri ag site.

A tornado touched down less than a mile west of Westphalia in northwest Osage County.  A couple of large tree limbs were blown down in this location.  The tornado travelled to the north northeast across U.S. Highway 63 to about 1.5 miles north of Westphalia, where it caused minor damage to two homes and downed large tree branches.  The tornado continued to move to the north northeast crossing the Maries River.  Tree damage was observed along the southern shore of the river.  The tornado then moved across a large flood plain and struck a large cluster of oak and cedar trees at a farmstead on a ridge.  Some of the oak trees were three feet in diameter and were either uprooted or snapped at the base.  There were a couple of small utility buildings that were destroyed northeast of this area.  There was also a row of cedar trees blown down to the northeast showing a convergent pattern.  The damage width over this area was 60 yards and the damage was rated EF1.  The tornado continued to skip and partially grazed a second farmstead and damaged two small buildings and trees.  The tornado continued to skip across U.S. Highway 50 approximately half a mile west of Loose Creek before it ended on County Road 412, about a mile northwest of Loose Creek.  The total damage track was 6.6 miles long.

A tornado touched down one mile north of Highway 94 on Highway PP.  Several large tree branches were blown down in this location.  A small utility building was damaged on a farmstead along Highway PP.  The tornado continued to move to the north northeast for about eight tenths of a mile before lifting and dissipating.  It was rated EF0 with a max damage width of 40 yards.

A tornado touched down on the western and northern sides of South Callaway High School and Elementary School.  The tornado initially hit the west side of the football stadium damaging the stands.  The tornado then moved north northeastward and caused minor damage to the northern part of the roof of the elementary school.  Additional damage occurred on the western side of the softball field in which the two dugouts were destroyed and the fence surrounding the baseball field was damaged.  A number of trees were uprooted west of the baseball field.  The tornado was travelling uphill and crossed Highway C approximately one and a half miles northwest of Mokane.  Additional minor tree damage was found off of Highway VV approximately 3.5 miles north of Mokane before lifting and dissipating.  The tornado had a max width of 40 yards, a path length of 3.7 miles and was rated EF0.

Up to two inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding. Several roads were flooded including the bridge on Buford Blvd., on the north side of Fredericktown, which had water flowing over it due to a nearby creek overflowing its banks.
A large sign was blown down at the intersection of Highway 163 and S. Bennett Drive.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees and a power pole was snapped off.
Golfball sized hail damaged a greenhouse at Clopton High School and also caused siding and roof damage to several buildings on campus.
A tornado briefly touched down in a field. No damage or injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a power pole and a couple of large trees on the southeast side of Greenville.  One tree fell onto an unoccupied car, causing extensive damage.

Between 2 and 5 inches of rain fell in a two hour period on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Illinois Route 37 near Kinmundy.  Several cars were swept downstream in a couple of spots in the northern half of the county, but the occupants were rescued with no injuries reported. Also, several basements in Kinmundy and Sandoval were flooded.

Between 3 and 5 inches of rain fell in a two hour period onto already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded over far southeastern Fayette County, including two feet of water over Illinois Route 37 in Farina.
A tornado briefly touched down in a field.  No damage was reported.
A tornado briefly touched down in a field.  No damage was reported.
A tornado briefly touched down in a field. No damage was reported.
A tornado briefly touched down in a field. No damage was reported.

Between 2 and 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including U.S. Highway 50 just west of California and Highway O just north of California.  One foot of water was flowing over Parkview Drive in California.
A tornado briefly touched down in a field.  No damage was reported.
Between 2 and 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded in Columbia.

The tornado touched down approximately 0.3 of a mile north of Dougherty Ferry Road near Lynkirk Rd. and moved north northwest through part of a subdivision.  The tornado lifted briefly, then touched down again near the intersection of Ballas Rd. and Kirk Place Dr. before lifting and disspating just east of West County Mall.  The path was approximately six tenths of a mile long and a maximum width around 300 yards across part of the subdivision and an average width of less than 200 yards elsewhere.  Widespread tree damage and minor roof damage was observed across the subdivision but the overall lack of structural damage suggests winds did not exceed 70 to 80 mph.  In the subdivision, several large healthy trees were uprooted and some roofs had missing or damaged shingles. At least one healthy tree was snapped several feet above its base.  More extensive tree damage was observed with the second touchdown near Ballas Rd. and Kirk Place Dr. where several healthy pine trees were snapped at the midpoint and the debris pattern indicated a convergent circulation.  Tree damage in this area also downed several powerlines along Ballas Road.
Several large tree limbs blown down.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees, tree limbs and power lines.  Some shingles were blown off of roofs, with additional roof damage caused by falling trees and tree limbs.

Between one and three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded in and around Ashland.  Also, several roads in the Sturgeon area were flooded including the intersection of Highway CC and Tri City Lake Road.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including water over a one lane bridge on Meadows Ford Road just south of intersection with Scruggs Station Road.
An eight inch diameter tree was blown down a the intersection of Illinois Routes 143 and 3.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several power lines in town.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway J about 4 miles east of Bethel.  It had between 4 and 6 inches of water flowing over it in several locations.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway C near South Callaway High School.  Also, U.S. Highway 54 had water over it in spots.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway K east of Laddonia and portions of Highway 19.

A tornado touched down about 4 miles west of Cook Station and paralled/crossed Highway YY several times before lifting and dissipating about 3 miles west northwest of Cook Station.  Damage was observed at the Carr Cemetery and the High Adventure Game Ranch.  Damage consisted of snapped and uprooted trees and downed branches.  The worst damage was at the Carr Cemetery where a number of large healthy oak trees were snapped just above the base.

The tornado crossed into Jefferson county about 3 miles northwest of Fletcher.  The tornado travelled northeast crossing just north of Morse Mill on State Highway B.  The tornado continued northeast passing through Lake Tishomingo, finally lifting 1.5 miles southwest of Otto.  The tornado snapped and uprooted numerous trees and downed numerous tree limbs along the entire path.  There were several areas of more substantial damage.  On Brook Hollow Lane, 3 miles north northwest of Fletcher, a home was damaged with part of the roof removed and a wall of the garage destroyed.  Also, on Brook Hollow Lane, a manufactured home sustained roof, siding and window damage.  Another area of damage was along Highway B just north of the Big River.  An outbuilding of the Morse Mill Baptist Church had the overhead doors caved in, which caused the roof to be removed and parts of the exterior walls to fail.  The last area of significant damage was at Lake Tishomingo, especially along the north shore.  Several of the homes suffered damage to the roofs and porches.  Also, a number of homes were damaged when trees fell on them.  No injuries were reported.

A tornado touched down about a mile and a quarter south southeast of Kimmswick on the Illinois side of the Mississippi River.  It travelled to the northeast for about 7 miles before lifting and dissipating.   Several large trees were blown down just west the levee in a two and a half mile area along the path.  The greatest degree of damage occurred on County Road 200E just south of the intersection with Merrimac Road.  The roof of a two story home was approximately 80 percent removed.  A second roof  to a porch was totally removed and blown to the north northeast.  Window and siding damage was also observed.  Several trees and large limbs at the back of this home were severely damaged and helped to show a large convergent damage pattern.  Two other homes west of the first home sustained varying degrees of damage.  Roof, window and siding damage was common on these two homes.  A large hanger at Jacobs Field, northeast of the home damage, sustained varying degrees of damage.  Large sections of the hanger's metal roof were blown a quarter to half a mile to the north northeast.  The tornado continued to damage small to medium sized machine sheds and caused minor damage to a few homes along the rest of its path.  No injuries were reported.

A tornado briefly touched down on Deer Hill Road, about 1.5 miles southwest of the intersection of Deer Hill Road and County Road HH.  A few large trees and several large tree limbs were blown down.  One home in the path of this tornado sustained shingle damage.

A tornado touched down in eastern Washington county about 4 miles northwest of Fletcher and travelled to the northeast.  It blew down several large trees before crossing into Jefferson county, about 3 miles northwest of Fletcher.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees near Highway M about one and a half miles north northeast of Cook Station.

A tornado briefly touched down on a ranch about 4 miles southwest of Annapolis.  Numerous large trees were twisted and blown down.  One of the trees fell onto a shed causing moderate damage.  No injuries were reported.

Up to 2 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded and a small creek in Steelville rose out of its banks blocking access to a bridge in town.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time onto already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including the southbound lanes Highway 141 under the Interstate 44 overpass, as well as Lewis Road north of Interstate 44.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous large tree limbs, a few large trees and caused moderate damage to an outbuilding.  Part of the roof was blown off and two walls had siding blown off.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs in Knob Lick.

The tornado initially touched down near the intersection of Duke Drive and Blackberry Avenue in University City.  The tornado traveled northwest producing intermittent damage for approximately 0.6 of a mile.  The damage became more continuous for the next 2.4 miles from just southeast of Olive Boulevard to near Dawes Place just southeast of Lackland Road.  Intermittent damage continued beyond Lackland Road to the northwest for an additional 1.4 miles.  The last discernible damage was located near St. Ann Lane.  The vast majority of the damage along the path consisted of varying degrees of tree damage which included numerous tree branches broken, trees uprooted, and tree trunks snapped well above their base.  The most significant structural damage occurred on Wallis Avenue just north of Trescott Avenue where a three foot diameter tree caved in the corner of a home.  The tornado reached a maximum width of 325 yards as it crossed Trescott Avenue.  This is also where the damage was most intense with wind speeds estimated at 85 mph.  Other notable damage was located near the intersection of Woodson Road and Harney Road where there was roof damage to a storage facility.  Minor structural damage was noted at other locations along the path caused by tree limbs or trees falling on homes.  Any direct tornadic damage to homes and businesses was minor superficial damage which consisted of siding, soffit and shingles.  No injuries were reported.

There was a wide swath of sporadic damage due to thunderstorm winds which occurred over portions of Webster Groves.  One area occurred along East Lockwood Avenue.  At the Eden Theological Seminary, a large rotted tree was blown down along with several large branches.  Several trees were also damaged on the northwest corner of the Webster University campus.  Another large tree branch was down near the bus stop at the corner of East Lockwood Ave. and Bompart Avenue.  Around three fourths of a mile further north, a large tree fell onto a house near the corner of North Bompart Ave. and Greeley Ave.  Two blocks further to the north near the corner of North Bompart Ave. and Clark Ave., a large tree fell on a wooden deck which contained a storage room.  A car and the corner of an adjacent house were also damaged.  All other damage found during the survey consisted of small downed tree limbs.
Hail was covering the ground.

The hail caused crop damage at the Eilerman Brothers Orchard just north of Batchtown.  The hail destroyed most of the asparagus, tomato, broccoli and egg plant fields.  No damage estimate was available.

Thunderstorm winds blew down 15 power poles onto Illinois Route 159 just north of Mansholt Road.  Route 159 was closed for about 12 hours while the poles were being replaced.  Additional power poles were blown down just north of Illinois Route 138 on Whitefield Road.

Damaging downburst winds totally destroyed a machine shed on Highway T, approximately 5 miles south southwest of Knox City.  The debris field from the machine shed extended southeast in a narrow corridor 40 yards wide and one mile long.  The narrow corridor of enhanced winds were estimated around 100 mph.  Other tree damage was found half a mile north of the intersection of Highway T and County Road 296.  A few large trees were uprooted while many large branches were blown down to the southeast.  A little further to the east, about three quarters of a mile north of the intersection of Highway E with Highway T, a machine shed was damaged.  There were indications that the machine shed flexed and shifted when the high winds hit and this flexing produced ripples in the sheet metal siding.  Other damage was noted to the soffiting on the building and one large overhead door was blown to the northeast.  On the same farmstead, the high winds caused a silo to be destroyed with the debris from the silo causing the collapse and destruction of two additional silos.
Thunderstorm winds knocked down a power pole on Highway T just south of Highway 6.

Downburst winds destroyed a machine shed in an open field about a quarter mile east of the intersection of Highway DD and County Road 204.  A little further to the east, a barn was destroyed.  The debris from this barn extended half a mile to the east southeast.

Downburst winds caused extensive damage on the south side of Lewistown.  A narrow corridor of enhanced winds, approximately 40 yards wide extended from the western edge of the town, between Monticello and Arbell Streets to Elm Street to the east.  Two mobile homes located west of Cherry Street were completely destroyed.  There were no occupants in either mobile home. A radio tower outside of the Lewistown Fire Station, which is on Cherry Street, was blown down.  A number of trees and large tree limbs were blown down in the area.  Pieces of the first mobile home were wrapped around one large tree trunk east of Cherry Street while much of the second mobile home was partially wrapped around and pushed against a large tree.  The home east of this point was protected by a large tree from much of the mobile home debris.  Winds were estimated around 100 mph in this area.  South of Arbell Street to the far southeastern part of town, damaging downburst winds were observed.  A few large trees fell on homes over this area.  A window was blown out on the Lewis County C-1 school on State Route J near the intersection with County Road 208.  The downburst wind damage area extended a bit further east to S. Oak Street.  No injuries were reported and no damage estimate was available.
Numerous reports of one inch to one and three quarters of an inch hail in an area from 4 miles east of Union through Villa Ridge and Gray Summit.

Up to two inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Several roads were closed due to flooding including U.S. Highway 50 on the eastern side of Gerald.

Up to two inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Several creeks rose well above their banks, affecting nearby roads, including Creve Coeur Creek and Two Mile Creek.
Between two and three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Dripping Springs Road at the intersection with Stone Drive.
A swath of large hail fell across Columbia ranging in size from an inch to one and three quarters of an inch in diameter.

Several inches of rain fell on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Several roads were closed due to flooding including Blackfoot Road on the north side of Columbia and Tri-City Lake Road at intersection with Highway CC, west of Centralia.
Over three inches of rain fell on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Route E south of Knox City and State Route 151 near Novelty.

Thunderstorm winds blew down several 14 to 16 inch diameter tree limbs on the east side of Chesterfield.  Also, the winds blew off part of the roof of a small storage building just north of Lambert Field.

Between 2 and 3 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Harris Lane between Fosterburg Road and Seminary Street.

Between 1 and 3 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including County Roads C and N near Bourbon, as well as low water crossings on County Road AA and TT.

A line of storms moved northwestward through the area. Thunderstorm winds blew down two trees onto U.S. Highway 50 just east of Mount Sterling and a couple of trees onto Highway 100 near the intersection with County Road N, just southeast of Morrison.

Between 3 and 5 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including U.S. Highway 40 east of Brownstown and U.S. Highway 51 just south of Shobonier.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs on government facility grounds near 2nd Street and Arsenal Street.
Thunderstorm winds blew over a semi truck just north of St. Louis Downtown Airport (KCPS) on Sauget Business Blvd.  No injuries were reported.

Lightning struck a tree on the southwest side of Forest Park.  Part of the tree fell onto an occupied car.  Three people were in the car at the time.  Two people sustained minor injuries, with one of them being take to the hospital nearby for observation.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree, as well as several large tree limbs, onto Skinker Boulevard near Fauquier Drive, blocking it for a time.
Three people were struck by lightning in the parking lot of St. Vincent County Park.  All sustained minor injuries and were taken to local hospitals for observation.
Thunderstorm winds blew part of the roof off on a lumber yard building.  Also, a power pole in the area was snapped off near the base.  It was a very limited area of wind damage.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree onto County Road 16 just southwest of Oakdale.

At 245 am, a young woman was travelling west of County Road 195th, when the car she was driving in went into water covering the road due to the North Fabius River, which was in flood.  The car became completely submerged and she perished.  The North Fabius River was at 21.16 feet at the time of the accident, over ten feet above flood stage, which is 11 feet.  The river crested later that morning at 22.19 feet around 1030 am.  This is the second highest crest since the gage was installed in June of 2005.

Thunderstorm winds caused some minor to major damage.  Several large trees were blown over.  One very large tree fell onto a two story barn one mile west of Camp Point, destroying the front half of it.  In Camp Point several trees were blown down in Bailey Park.  Further to the east, about a mile south of Clayton, the thunderstorm winds blew off part of the roof of a house causing moderate damage as well as water damage to portions of the house.  A large tree in this location fell down, crushing a swing set.  No injuries were reported.

Thunderstorm winds blew down a couple of trees and large tree limbs in Timewell.  One large tree limb fell onto a car causing moderate damage, one landed on a garage destroying it and several landed on roofs causing minor damage.  In Mount Sterling, a couple of trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.  No injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a power line in town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees, tree limbs and power lines in town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees in town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree, several tree limbs and power lines in town.  The tree knocked down a power pole as it fell causing a power outage.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree onto Illinois Route 96 about half a mile north of Interstate 72, blocking it for awhile.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a couple of large trees about 2 miles west southwest of Japan.
Thunderstorm winds blew down two large trees on the east side of town blocking a road for awhile.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils, causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including a secondary road near the intersection of U.S. Highway 50 and State Highway 89, just east of Linn. Also, Highway N in Freedom was closed due to flooding, as well as Highway W just north of Linn.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded with some having between 6 and 8 inches of flowing water over them, mainly east of Mount Sterling.

Up to 5 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time on already saturated soils causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded and a couple of roads and culverts were washed out. National Weather Service personnel conducted a damage survey over parts of west central Osage county and determined that the tree and structural damage was due to a combination of damaging downburst winds and microbursts from a severe thunderstorm which moved through the area between 620 pm and 630 pm.||The damage area started a quarter of a mile west of County Road 608 near the Maries River.  The roof of one machine shed was uplifted to the southeast on a farmstead near County Road 608.  Tree damage was confined at three locations along the Maries River.  One area of tree damage extended from the river up to the ridge axis across the river.  Several large oak and pecan trees were damaged in this area.||Other nearby tree damage due to the downbursts occurred along Brush Creek Hollow about 2 miles south southwest of Loose Creek.  Several large oak trees over 100 years old were uprooted due to an intense microburst.  Surface wind gusts were estimated between 85 and 95 mph in this location.||Further east, towards the south end of County Road 603, near Brush Creek, a second machine shed was completely destroyed with the debris from the shed laid to the west southwest.  As the machine shed started to lift to the west, five occupants moved inside a large pickup truck within the machine shed.  None of the occupants were injured.  A nearby house, approximately 50 yards to the south, was not damaged.  Approximately 100 to 150 yards northeast and east of the machine shed, several large hardwood trees were uprooted and also lying to the west and southwest.  This is an interesting area in which the tree and machine shed damage laid to the west and southwest and occurred immediately on the back side (west side) of the severe thunderstorm. This is an uncommon type of damage pattern.  Surface winds were estimated between 70 and 90 mph in this location.||The final area of tree damage occurred 2.2 miles southeast of the town of Loose Creek, along County Road 602.  This road was along a ridge axis and several very large oak trees were uprooted to the northeast.||The total tree and structural damage area extended 5 miles in length and one mile in width.
