Thunderstorm winds caused a carport to collapse in Clayton.
Up to five inches of rain fell over Shelby County in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway 151 just north of Clarence.

Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time over Lewis County causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including the intersection of Route D and Highway 156, just east of Newark.
Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time over Bond County causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including streets in Greenville.

Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time over St. Clair County causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including roads in Scott AFB with 6 to 18 inches of water over them.  Highway 13, near intersection with Highway 157, was closed due to 6 feet of water over the road under a railroad viaduct.
Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time over Monroe County causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including portions of Bluff Road and Brandt Road.

Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time over portions of Iron County causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded.  Highway 49 just south of Viburnum was washed away by the flood waters.  Also, Highway 21 was impassable in spots.

Up to five inches of rain fell in a 24 hour period.  This caused flash flooding on Joachim Creek in DeSoto.  The creek rose quickly and numerous roads on the east side of town were flooded.  The water rose high enough that the fire station on East Miller Street had over a foot of water in it throughout the offices and engine room.  About 125 homes were affected by the flash flooding.  Also, an 80 year old woman drove into the flood waters on Veterans Drive.  Despite attempts by emergency workers to block the car, it plunged into the rushing creek with the woman inside.  Several hours later the water receded enough for the emergency workers to find her body in the vehicle a little ways downstream.
Thunderstorm winds snapped off four power poles along Old Highway 100, near intersection with Highway T.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees near the intersection of Highway 94 and Highway DD.
Thunderstorm winds blew over a few trees.
Thunderstorm winds snapped off a tree.  Also, there was minor roof and gutter damage to one house.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees and power lines.  One tree was blocking New Halls Ferry Road near intersection with Douglas Road.
Large hail fell in a swath from the northeast side of Columbia to Murry.  Some of the large hail caused minor damage to a few vehicles.
Several large tree limbs were blown down.

A tornado touched down west southwest of Hannibal, damaging several trees and a structure about a mile south of the Hannibal Regional Medical Center, just northeast of the intersection of Centerville Road and County Road 420. The tornado then moved northeast and caused its most intense damage, low end EF-1, at the intersection of Centerville Road and Shinn Lane.  In this area several large trees were either uprooted or snapped off halfway up the trunk.  The tornado moved northeast to Highway MM where it tore about a quarter of the tin roof off of a farm building and damaged some trees.  The tornado dissipated as it crossed Highway MM.

A line of severe thunderstorms moved through Hannibal.  The storms caused considerable wind damage in and around Hannibal.  The damage area was roughly from Highway MM north to Hannibal-LaGrange University.  One building at the university had a small portion of its roof torn off.  Numerous trees were either uprooted or snapped along Palmyra Road/Mark Twain Avenue.  A three story brick building in downtown Hannibal on Main Street had a wall collapse and about half its roof torn off.  Wind gusts in this area were likely around 100 mph.  Tree damage was common west of the downtown area to U.S. Highway 61 and then west of U.S. Highway 61 along West Ely Road.  The subdivisions around Pioneer Lake and Apollo Lake had numerous large tree branches blown down.  One home near Apollo Lake had windows broken by flying debris.  A small building lost part of its roof on the south side of Hannibal on Market Street.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous large tree limbs along Highway J and Highway A.

A line of severe thunderstorms moved through northern portions of Pike County.  Considerable wind damage was noted along the I-72 corridor from the Mississippi River to the I-72/I-172 interchange.  There was a great deal of tree damage on both sides of the road where it extended from the eastern bank of the river to the levee.  Varying sizes of limbs and branches were broken, twisted and dangling.  The damage extended well beyond the levee.  Three residences on the north side of the interstate near the first Illinois exit had minor roof damage.  Further east, the winds destroyed a large machine shed at a farmstead.  The next farm along the north side of the road suffered the worst damage.  This property consisted of 7 small grain bins and 4 large ones.  The smaller bins are set to the west of the larger ones.  All 11 grain bins were dented on the southwest side to some degree.  By far the worst was the southwestern most large grain bin.  It was completely crushed to the point where it is a total loss.  The interstate bends to the northeast just past the farm with the grain bins.  There was some tree damage to the next two residences on the south side of the interstate prior to the interchange with I-172.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor damage to a garage in Payson.  Also, several power poles were snapped and a couple of trees uprooted in Payson.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a few large trees.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree.
There were several reports of one inch hail in St. Peters, Harvester and St. Charles.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several power lines at the intersection of Bryan Road and Mexico Road.
Thunderstorm winds snapped a couple of large trees in Winchester.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  At the intersection of Highway C and Green Acres Drive, over a foot of water covered the road, so the road was closed for awhile.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs in Plainview.

Thunderstorm winds blew off the decorative steel portion of a grocery store roof in Staunton.  The main roof remained intact with just minor leaks into the store below.  Also, several trees and power lines were blown down around town.
Thunderstorm winds snapped off a two foot diameter tree at its base.

A tornado touched down in the downtown portion of Mt. Olive and traveled to the east.  The damage path was 4 blocks long and ranged from 50 to 75 yards wide.  The second story of a brick building was blown off.  Large sections of several roofs were blown 2 blocks to the north.  A historic 2 story home had the roof blown off and windows were blown out of several homes and businesses.  Three people sustained minor injuries.

Thunderstorm winds caused minor damage to the fire station roof.  A small shed behind the fire station was destroyed.  Also, several large trees were uprooted and a couple others were snapped off.  A small ham radio tower behind a house was bent.

During the evening of Friday April 22nd, an intense supercell thunderstorm produced a long-track tornado which tore a path of destruction from west to east across the St. Louis Metropolitan Area, from St. Louis County Missouri eastward through the far northern portions of the City of St. Louis, then across the Mississippi River into Madison County Illinois. The tornado reached a maximum intensity of EF4 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale as it tracked through the community of Bridgeton, just west of Lambert St. Louis International Airport, in St. Louis County. The total path length was 21.3 miles, with a width of up to half a mile.||As the tornado crossed from St. Louis County into the far northern portions of the City of St. Louis, there was EF-1 tree damage and minor roof and siding damage which was rated EF-0.  The tornado continued to travel to the east and crossed the Mississippi River into Madison County Illinois, approximately 1.5 miles south of Interstate 270.
The Illinois River At La Grange set a new record reaching 34.50 feet on April 27th. The river remained above flood stage into May. Agriculture lowland damage was the only know damage.
The Illinois River hit major flood levels from Meredosia to Valley City south into Calhoun County. In Pike County the river crested on April 27th, but remained above flood stage into May.

The Illinois River hit major flood levels all along the border of Calhoun County. The river crested at Hardin, IL on April 26th at 36.34 feet but remained over flood stage into May.|Agricultural damage was the only know damage. Damage estimates were not available.

The Kaskaskia River in Fayette County hit major flood levels. The river crested at Vandalia at 27.91 feet on April 19th. The river fell below flood stage on April 30th. The was little known damage except for agricultural lowlands.

The La Moine River along the border of Brown County hit major flood levels. The river crested at Ripley on April 21st at a new record of 32.54 feet. The river fell below flood stage on April 26. Damage was limited to agricultural lowlands.

The Mississippi River reached major flood levels along the border of Adams County. The river crested at most locations on April 21st but remained above flood stage into May. Damage was limited to agricultural lowlands.

The Mississippi River reached major flood levels along the border of Pike County. The river crested on April 21st and 22nd, but remained above flood stage into May. Damage was limited to a few closed roads and agricultural lowlands.

The Mississippi River reached major flood levels along the border of Calhoun County. The river crested on April 22nd and 23rd but remained above flood stage into May. Damage was limited to a few closed roads and agricultural lowlands.
The Mississippi River reached major flood levels along the border of Jersey County. The river crested on April 25th, but remained above flood stage into May. Damage was limited to a few closed roads.

The Mississippi River rose to major flood levels along the Marion County border. The river crested on April 21st, but remained above flood stage into May. Damage was limited to a few roads closed and agricultural lowlands.

The Mississippi River rose to major flood levels along the border of Ralls County. The river crested on the 21st through 22nd,  but continued above flood stage into May. Damage was limited to a few roads closed and flooding of agricultural lowlands.

The Mississippi River rose to major flood levels along the border of Pike County. The river crested on the 22nd but remained above flood stage into May. The City of Clarksville, with the help of the Missouri National Guard and many volunteers, was able to build a sandbag wall to protect the downtown business district. Thus damage was limited to some flooded roads, a few outbuilding in the flood plain, and agricultural lowlands.

The Mississippi River rose to major flood levels along the border with Lincoln County. The river crested on 23rd, but remained above flood stage into May. The only major damage occurred in Winfield. A levee failure resulted in the flooding of about 20 homes on the east side of Highway 79 in the Winfield Acres area.

The Mississippi River rose to major flood levels along the border of St. Charles County. The river crested on April 25th but remained above flood stage into May. Flooding at the St. Charles Smartt Field Airport caused the National Weather Service to remove the Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS). Damage was limited to fishing cabins along the river, some road closures, and agricultural lowlands.

The Mississippi River rose to major flood levels along the border of Lewis County. The river crested on April 21st, but remained above flood stage into May. Damage was limited to a few roads closed and agricultural lowlands.
The North Fabius River rose to major flood levels in Lewis County. The river crested on April 20th. Damage was limited to some closed roads and flooded farmland.
The Middle Fabius River rose to major flood levels. The river crested on April 20th. Damage was limited to a few closed roads and flooded farmland.
The South Fabius River crested at major flood level on April 19th.
The North River crested at major flood level on April 18th. Damage was limited to a few closed roads and flooded farmland.

The Illinois River at LaGrange remained in flood at major flood levels in early May, dropping below flood stage on the 22nd at 0600 CST. The river then rose again into flood on the on the 28th and continued in flood into June.

The Illinois River along the border of Pike County remained at major flood levels in early May, dropping below flood stage on the 23rd, then rose to major levels again at the end of the month. The river remained in flood into June.

The Illinois River along the border of Greene County remained at major flood levels in early May, dropped below major levels for a while, then rose to major levels again at the end of May. Damage was limited to some closed roads and flooded farmland.

The Illinois River along the border of Calhoun County remained at major flood levels in early May, dropped below major levels for a while, then rose to major levels again at the end of May. Damage was limited to some closed roads and flooded farmland.

The Illinois River along the border of Jersey County remained at major flood levels in early May, dropped below major levels for a while, then rose to major levels again at the end of May. Damage was limited to some closed roads and flooded farmland.
The Illinois River hit major flood levels along the border of Greene County. The river crested around the 27th, but remained at major flood levels into May.
The Illinois River hit major flood levels along the border of Jersey County. The river crested around the 27th, but remained at major flood levels into May.

The Mississippi River along the border of Adams County continued at major flood levels into early May. The river gradually fell and dropped below flood stage on the 23rd, only to rise over flood stage on the 27th and hit major flood levels again at the end of May. Major flooding continued into early June.

The Mississippi River was at major flood levels in early May, dropped a bit for the middle of the month, then rose to major flood levels again at the end of the month. Damage was limited to some flooded roads and flooded farmland.

The Mississippi continued in flood along the border of Marion County through May. The river started at major flood levels, dropped some in the middle of the month, but then rose again to major levels at the end of May. The flood wall in Hannibal kept the tourist areas nice and dry. Damage was limited to some closed roads and flooded farmland.

The Mississippi River remained in flood through May along the border of Pike County. The river started at major flood levels, dropped some into the middle of the month, then rose again to major levels at the end of May. The town most affected was Clarksville. Sandbagging efforts by the National Guard and volunteers were successful in keeping the downtown area mostly dry.
The Illinois River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 6th. The river then slowly fell dropping below flood stage on the 23rd. Damage was minimal.
The Illinois River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 6th. The river then slowly fell dropping below flood stage on the 28th. Damage was minimal.
The Illinois River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 4th - 6th. The river remained in flood into July. Damage was minimal.
The Illinois River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 4th. The river remained in flood into July.
The Illinois River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 4th. The river remained in flood into July.
The Mississippi River bordering St. Clair County started June in flood and rose to major flood levels cresting on the 4th. The river fell below flood stage on the 15th. Damage was minimal.

The Mississippi River bordering Adams County started June in flood and rose to major flood levels cresting on the 1st. The river fell below flood stage on the 20th. Damage was limited to some closed roads and flooded farmland.

The Mississippi River bordering on Pike County started June in flood and rose to major flood levels cresting on the 1st. The river remained in flood into July. Damage was limited to a few closed roads and flooded farmland.
The Mississippi River bordering Calhoun County started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting from June 2 - 4. The river remained in flood into July. Damage was minimal.

The Mississippi River bordering Jersey County started June in flood and rose to major flood levels cresting on the 4th. The river remained in flood into July. Damage was limited to a few closed roads.
The Mississippi River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 5th. The river fell below flood stage on the 26. Damage was limited to some closed roads and flooded farmland.
The Mississippi River bordering Madison County started June in flood and rose to major flood levels cresting on the 3rd. The river fell below flood stage on the 22nd. Damage was minimal.

The Mississippi River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 1st. The river fell below flood stage on the 21st. Damage was limited to some flooded roads and flooded farmland.
The Mississippi River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 1st. The river fell the rest of the month but remained in flood into July.

The Mississippi River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 1st. The river fell the rest of the month but remained in flood into July. Damage was mainly limited to some flooded roads and flooded farmland. Residents of Clarksville once again used the National Guard and volunteers to build a sandbag wall to keep the downtown business district dry.

The Mississippi River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 2nd. The river fell the rest of the month but remained in flood into July. Damage was limited to some flooded roads and flooded farmland.

The Mississippi River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 4rd. The river fell most of the rest of June but remained in flood into July. Damage was limited to some flooded roads, and flooded farmland and parks.
The Missouri River started June in flood and hit major flood levels cresting on the 2nd. The river fell below flood stage on the 5th. Damage was limited to some flooded roads and flooded farmland.
The Missouri River started the month in flood and rose to major flood levels cresting on the 2nd. The river then fell dropping below flood stage on the 7th.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a 10 inch diameter tree across Highway 49, just northwest of Viburnum.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs just south of Potosi.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous large tree limbs as well as several power lines in Bonne Terre and Park Hills.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several power lines around town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a two foot diameter tree.  The tree then knocked down a nearby power line.

Up to 5 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Highway N about a mile east of intersection with Highway K.  Highway 94 had over 10 inches of water over it near intersection with First Capitol Drive.  Several cars became stuck in the water at the intersection.
Up to 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded, especially in Carlinville and Girard.

Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including U.S. Highway 40 between I-70 and Midway.  Red Rock Road was washed out by the flood waters where it crosses Reeder Creek.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding in the Hannibal and Palmyra areas.  Several roads were flooded including the intersection of U.S. Highway 61 and Highway 168.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Bear Creek was running out of its banks and flooding a mobile home park on the south side of Hannibal just off of Warren Barrett Drive on Ledbetter Lane.  Also, Highway 79 near intersection with Monkey Run Trail had water flowing over it.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a one foot diameter tree as well as numerous tree limbs in Foley.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree on the south side of Hamburg.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several medium to large trees around Fredericktown.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees and power lines along County Road 163 just northeast of Des Arc.
Thunderstorm winds blew down two large trees, partially blocking Highway F near intersection with Highway MM.
Thunderstorm winds split a three foot diameter tree and blew down numerous large tree limbs around town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs on the north side of Chester.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a 12 inch diameter tree limb which fell on top of a building at a car dealership.
Thunderstorm winds blew over a large tree in O'Fallon.  Also, the ASOS unit at Scott Air Force Base recorded at 67 MPH wind gust with the storms.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several medium to large trees as well as several power lines around town.  A few shingles were blown off of a couple of homes.
Thunderstorm winds snapped a large tree off at the ground.
Thunderstorm winds damaged several sheds in an area from just east of St. Libory to near Venedy.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a couple of trees as well as numerous tree limbs around town.  Also, several homes sustained minor shingle damage.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees in town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous large tree limbs around town.

Thunderstorm winds blew down a large walnut tree about 6 miles south of Taylor Springs.  Also, several large trees were blown down around Hillsboro.  One tree fell on top of an unoccupied vehicle, causing major damage.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees along Emmerson Airline Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous large tree limbs.
Two large trees were blown down, which in turn knocked down a couple of power lines.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees just east of Tipton and in California.
Thunderstorm winds snapped off several large trees across town.  Also, some shingles were blown off of a house south of town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a couple of trees which blocked both lanes of Highway 94 near Wainwright.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including State Highway MM where it goes over Fox Hollow Branch.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several power lines around town.
Thunderstorm wind blew down several large trees around town.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree onto an unoccupied car that was parked at the Historic Daniel Boone Home & Heritage Center.  The car sustained major damage.

Thunderstorm winds caused a wide swath of damage from about 2 miles north of Danville on Highway 161, eastward across the county to about 2 miles east of Highway 19.  Most of the damage was broken tree limbs, several large trees blown down or snapped off as well as major damage to two grain bins at the intersection of County Roads 219 and 220.  The grain bins were dented in considerably and the elevator legs had collapsed.

A weak tornado briefly touched down along Highway 161 from 2.5 miles south southwest to 2 miles south southwest of Montgomery City.  Much of the damage was confined to tree damage.  One large tree snapped about a third of the way from the base and fell onto a parked school bus.  No one was inside the bus.  Before the tornado lifted and dissipated, three power poles were bent about 40 degrees to the northeast.  Overall, the tornado path length was half a mile and max path width was 30 yards.  The damage was rated as EF0 with max winds of 75 MPH.

A weak tornado briefly touched down about two miles south of Montgomery City along Blue Bird Road.  Much of the damage was confined to tree damage.  Before lifting and dissipating near the intersection of Blue Bird Road and Bob White Road, the roof of an old machine shed was peeled off to the south.  The tornado path length was two tenths of a mile with a max path width of 30 yards.  The damage was rated EF0 with max wind speeds of 75 MPH.

A weak tornado touched down 2 miles north northwest of New Florence.  Much of the damage was confined to downed trees.  The tornado traveled east for about a mile.  Before lifting and dissipating, the tornado caused minor siding and soffit damage to a home and uprooted a large tree in the backyard.  The tornado path length was 1.06 miles with a max path width of 40 yards.  The damage was rated EF0 with max wind speeds of 80 MPH.

A tornado touched down just west of Highway UU, around 3.5 miles southwest of Union.  Most of the damage consisted of snapped and downed trees and broken tree limbs. Five homes located along Indian Prairie Lane between Union and St. Clair suffered minor roof damage. The tornado lifted and dissipated just south of the intersection of Meramec Terrace Road and Indian Acres Road, around 3.4 miles southwest of Robertsville.  The tornado path length was 10 miles with a max path width of 550 yards.  The damage was rated EF1 with max wind speeds of 105 MPH.

A tornado touched down in extreme western Jefferson County near Highway NN and Apke Lane.  It moved to the east and most of the damage consisted of snapped and downed trees and broken tree limbs.  In the Byrnes Mill area several mobile homes were damaged from fallen trees.  In Scotsdale, several school buildings at Our Lady Queen of Peace Church suffered minor damage.  The tornado lifted and dissipated west of Rustic Trails Drive, around 2.7 miles east of Byrnes Mill.  The tornado path length was 12.4 miles and the max path width was 200 yards.  The damage was rated EF1 with max wind speeds of 100 MPH.
One inch hail fell in Maryland Heights.
One inch hail fell in Florrisant.

The tornado began on the west side of Gillespie, causing minor damage to an apartment complex on the southwest side of the intersection of Broadway Street and LJ Avenue.  It blew out several windows on one of the apartment buildings.  It then caused major damage to the north end of a brick gymnasium at Gillespie High School.  The damage to the gymnasium was rated EF2.  Then it proceeded to travel northeast, blowing the roof off of a house just northeast of the high school.  Also, a large pine tree was snapped off at the base next to the house.  The tornado continued to the northeast.  There was extensive damage to trees and roofs along a west southwest to east northeast path through the town.  The tornado destroyed a garage at the corner of Henry Street and Fulton Street.  The tornado lifted and dissipated just north of the intersection of Harding Avenue and Illinois Route 16.  The tornado path length was 1.5 miles with max path width of 150 yards.  The damage was rated EF2 with max wind speeds of 115 MPH.

A tornado touched down half a mile north of the intersection of County Road 100E and 2200N or 3.5 miles south-southwest of Waggoner, Illinois.  Several large tree limbs 6 to 10 inches in diameter were blown down by the tornado. The tornado path at this location was 30 yards wide. The tornado traveled northeast and damaged one barn and a few outbuildings on Goby Avenue, about 1.5 miles west of I-55.  The roof of two outbuildings were uplifted and tossed 100 to 150 yards to the northeast.  Another outbuilding was severely damaged on Coalfield Avenue, half a quarter of a mile west of I-55. Damage intensity was rated EF1.  Debris from this machine shed was tossed across a corn field and across I-55. The tornado then crossed I-55, blowing over three tractor trailers.  No injuries were reported.  The tornado then damaged a third farmstead on County Road 2500N approximately a quarter of a mile east of I-55. Windows were blown inward on a two story farm home and two machine sheds were severely damaged. The damage intensity was rated EF1 and damage was 40 yards wide. The tornado continued to move northeast and downed large tree branches 6 to 10 inches in diameter on East Waggoner Road, about 2 miles east southeast of Waggoner, Illinois.  The tornado then lifted and dissipated.  The tornado path length was 4.3 miles with a max path width of 50 yards.  The damage was rated EF1 with max wind speeds estimated between 90 and 100 MPH.
A wide swath of wind damage occurred over northern Macoupin County.  Numerous trees and tree limbs were blown down.  Also, an outbuilding on the west side of Virden had part of its roof blown off.

A wide swath of wind damage occurred over far northern Montgomery County.  Several outbuilding sustained minor to moderate damage.  Five grain bins were blown off their foundations into a field on Thomasville Trail, about half a mile west of I-55.  Also, several large trees and numerous tree limbs were blown down.
Thunderstorm winds snapped several power poles in Sorento.  Just north of Greenville, several large trees were snapped and numerous tree limbs were blown down.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree limb onto U.S. Highway 51 about a mile north of Vandalia.

A tornado touched down in the Columbia Bottom Conservation Area, about 3 miles northeast of the interchange of I-270 and Columbia Bottom Road.  It uprooted a large tree in this location, then traveled to the northeast.  It uprooted another large tree just northeast of Upper Columbia Bottom Road, before turning a bit more easterly and crossed the Mississippi River into Madison County Illinois.  For this segment of the tornado, the path length in St. Louis County was 2 miles with a max path width of 50 yards.  The damage for this segment was rated EF1 with max wind speeds of 90 MPH.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 10.6 miles with a max path width of 150 yards.  The tornado was rated EF3 with max wind speeds of 160 MPH.

The tornado crossed the Mississippi River from St. Louis County Missouri into Madison County Illinois, about 1.1 miles northwest of the intersection of Illinois Routes 3 and 203.  It blew down several trees once it made landfall.  As it traveled to the east northeast, it took about a quarter of the roof off of a business on the northwest corner of the intersection of Illinois Route 3 and Piasa Lane.  On the east side of Illinois Route 3, a gas station sustained minor damage.  Damage in this area was rated EF1.  Further northeast, several power poles were snapped along S. Delmar Avenue.  Just south of the intersection of Robbins Road and Illinois Route 111, 5 large wooden power poles were snapped and there was a convergent pattern in the tree damage to the north.  As it crossed the far southern portions of South Roxana, there was minor damage to several homes, then the tornado crossed Highway 255. It buckled in a wall on a large steel framework building and twisted the roof steel girders just south of Old Alton Edwardsville Road, about a quarter of a mile east of the intersection of Old Alton Edwardsville Road and Section Line Road.  On the same property, another very large and well-built wood framed metal sided storage building was completely destroyed by the tornado.  Damage was rated EF3 in this location.  The tornado continued to the northeast crossing Illinois Route 143 just north of the intersection with N. University Dr.  Before lifting and dissipating, the tornado crossed Illinois Route 159, just south of Fox Creek Golf Club and snapped off several large fir trees as well as a wooden power pole.  The tornado path length in Madison County was 8.6 miles with a max path width of 150 yards.  The damage in this segment was rated EF3 with max wind speeds of 160 MPH.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 10.6 miles with a max path width of 150 yards.  The tornado was rated EF3 with max wind speeds of 160 MPH.
Thunderstorm winds snapped off several large trees in southwestern St. Charles County between Highway DD and Highway 94.

A tornado touched down about four miles southwest of Weldon Spring in St. Charles County, Missouri. It downed trees, blew over empty tractor trailers, and caused minor damage to construction equipment. It moved east-northeast into Weldon Spring Heights and the Missouri Research Park (on the south side of Weldon Spring) causing roof, window, and solar panel damage to a few structures as well as downing more trees before crossing Interstate 64. The tornado passed within one half of a mile of the National Weather Service Weather Forecast Office which is located in the Missouri Research Park. The tornado continued moving east-northeast through densely populated residential areas of southern St. Charles County, south of Highway 94. Roofing was torn off of Bryan Middle School and blown 100 yards, many houses suffered varying degrees of roof (from minor damage to removal of entire roof), wall (from minor damage to total collapse), and overall structural damage, and thousands of trees were damaged. The most intense damage, rated EF3, occurred on Haversham Drive where only the interior walls were left standing of three homes. The tornado began to move a bit more easterly, widening to nearly 1000 yards (or a half-mile), causing damage in residential areas and the St. Charles Family Arena before crossing the Missouri River into St. Louis County just south of Interstate 70.||The tornado caused damage to 765 homes in St. Charles County.  Seven hundred twenty-three homes suffered minor damage, 34 homes suffered major damage, and 8 homes were destroyed. Three hundred forty-eight businesses sustained minor damage, while 25 businesses had major damage. Cleanup costs alone for St. Charles County was 2.4 million dollars, with approximately 50,000 tons of tree and limb debris removed.  There were 8 minor injuries due to the tornado.||The path length of the tornado in St. Charles County was 14.8 miles with a max path width of 950 yards.  The damage for this segment was estimated to be EF3 with max wind speeds of 150 MPH.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 31.8 miles with a max path width of 1 mile and a maximum damage rating of EF3.

The tornado crossed the Missouri River from St. Charles County into St. Louis County just south of Interstate 70.  As it moved through the Riverport area, it caused major damage to one of the buildings at Hollywood Casino.  Part of the roof and most of the siding were torn off of a section of the casino that housed maintenance and staff offices.  Five large power poles were snapped off at the base. The damage in this area was rated EF2.  Also, numerous trees were snapped off.  Further to the east in the Riverport area, a gas station lost part of its canopy and a nearby hotel sustained minor roof damage as well as several windows blown out.  The tornado then crossed Interstate 70 into the Earth City area.  As it crossed the highway at the intersection of I-70 and Earth City Expressway it knocked down the large steel truss that holds signs for the east bound side of I-70 into the west bound lanes of the highway.  Traffic was backed up for hours in this area due to the fallen sign and numerous power lines as well as debris laying across the interstate.  North of I-70 the tornado widened to a mile wide with the most significant damage centered just northwest of the I-70/Earth City Expressway interchange.  One warehouse building had a section of the pre-cast concrete wall collapse outward and fall onto the parking lot on the southeast corner.  Meanwhile on the north facing side of the warehouse, several bay doors were blown in and several tractor trailers and delivery trucks were blown over.  The building next door had roof damage and an unoccupied car nearby was flipped onto its roof and another one was rolled as well.   The damage in this area was rated EF2.  Further to the east and northeast, the Point 70 office building sustained extensive window damage and another warehouse had a quarter of its roof peeled off.  Spectrum Brands warehouse building on Corporate Exchange Drive had a very large section of pre-cast concrete walls collapse inward and damage here was rated EF2.  The tornado continued to the east, crossing Interstate 270 between Interstate 70 and St. Charles Rock Road.  Numerous trees, power poles and power lines were blown down across Bridgeton.  An apartment building on Natural Bridge Road lost its entire roof with some of the debris landing on cars in the parking lot.  Several other apartment buildings had minor roof damage.  Damage in this area was rated EF2.  The tornado crossed the northern portions of Lambert-St. Louis International Airport, causing minor damage to four outbuildings.  From there the tornado continued east, blowing down or uprooting numerous large trees, power poles and power lines in Berkley, Kinloch, Ferguson, and Dellwood mainly along and north of Chambers Road.  Several of the large trees fell onto houses and vehicles causing minor to major damage.  As it crossed New Halls Ferry Road it began to go in a more east northeasterly direction, paralleling Interstate 270 for a time.  A gas station at the intersection of Dunn Road and Old Halls Ferry Road had one of its canopies collapsed.   Just east of Highway 367, six power poles were snapped off along Dunn Road on the north side of I-270.  A bit further east, just east of Bellefontaine Road, an apartment complex on N. Garden Drive had eight of its buildings sustain major roof damage.   Otherwise, most of the damage in the area was to trees and power lines.  A few of the trees landed on homes causing varying degrees of damage.  The tornado then lifted and dissipated on the banks of the Mississippi River about six tenths of a mile north northeast of the intersection of I-270 and Columbia Bottom Road. The tornado caused damage to 612 homes in St. Louis County.  Five hundred and ten homes suffered minor damage, 101 homes suffered major damage, and one home was destroyed. One hundred twenty-one businesses sustained minor damage, while 5 businesses had major damage. Cleanup costs alone for St. Louis County was 4.3 million dollars.||The path length of the tornado in St. Louis County was 17.0 miles with a max path width of a mile wide.  The damage for this segment was estimated to be EF2 with max wind speeds of 130 MPH.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 31.8 miles with a max path width of 1 mile and a maximum damage rating of EF3.

A wide swath of wind damage, just north of the path of the tornado that moved through St. Louis County extended from the I-270/Lindbergh Boulevard interchange eastward to the just west of the Mississippi River.  The most intense wind damage was to the Ramada Inn on the northeast side of the I-270/Lindbergh Boulevard interchange.  It lost about half its roof with some of the debris landing on cars in the parking lot destroying them.  More of the debris landed over two tenths of a mile away, damaging or destroying a number of campers and RVs at an RV business with a number of vehicles having 2x4s driven into them.  Another nearby hotel sustained moderate roof damage as well.  Otherwise, most of the wind damage consisted of trees blown over, numerous large tree limbs blown down, as well as power lines being blown down.  There was one injury to a hotel occupant at the Ramada Inn,  the person sustained a broken arm.

Thunderstorm winds blew down several very large trees around the 1000 block of both Grand Avenue and Randle Street near North Elm Street.  One of the trees went through the roof of a house on Grand Avenue causing major damage.  Another large tree on Randle Street pulled down several power lines.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree blocking the door to a house, trapping the occupant briefly.  There was only minor structural damage to the house.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor roof damage to a home at the intersection of New Poag Road and Illinois Route 111.
Thunderstorm winds blew over several tractor trailers along Interstate 55 between mile markers 31 and 28 on the southbound side of the highway.  No injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees around town as well as several fences.
Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads throughout the county were flooded, including several near Stone Hill Winery in Hermann.
Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including Highway 94.  Highway 94 was flooded in several locations.
Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Highway 135 was flooded in several spots southeast of the intersection with Highway T for about a four mile stretch.
Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding. Highway 135 was flooded in several spots southeast of the intersection with Highway T for about a four mile stretch.

Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Shawnee Ford Road, north northwest of Japan.  Also, Highway AC near Boone Creek Bridge had several feet of water over it.
Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Highway 94 and Highway B in southwestern Warren County.
Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding. Several roads were flooded including Aubuchon Road and Teson Road in north county and Theiss Road in south county.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Illinois Route 13 between Illinois Route 157 and Busch Boulevard.  One car drove into the flood waters and was partially submerged.  The occupant was rescued, but no injuries reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs and power lines around town.

Up to five inches of rain fell in about a three hour period.  Several roads were flooded including County Road 550N.  A man, along with his two year old son, tried to drive his car through 2 feet of flowing water on County Road 550N, about a mile and an half west of Illinois Route 107.  The vehicle was swept off the road. He managed to unbuckle his son from the car seat, but could not get a hold of him because of the rushing waters.  The man made it to dry ground.  The child's body was found the next morning about half a mile down stream.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a very short amount of time causing flash flooding, especially in southern portions of the city.  Flooding was reported in low lying areas along Hampton Avenue.  Also, at the intersection of S. Kingshighway Boulevard and where Tholozan Avenue heads east, there was over a foot of water with a car dealership flooded.  A couple blocks south on S. Kingshighway Boulevard at Chippewa Street, there was over two feet of water in that intersection.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a very short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including the intersection of Ladue Road and Spoede Road in Creve Coeur, as well as the intersection of Ladue Road and Graeser Road.  Also, Interstate 255 near Jefferson Barracks had water flowing across to the point traffic was stopped.  The intersection of South Fillmore and East Clinton Place was flooded in Kirkwood.  In Fenton, Highway 141 was flooded near interchange with Highway 30 and also where Highway 141 goes under Interstate 44.  In University City, the River Des Peres was out of its banks and flooding an apartment complex near the intersection of Olive Boulevard and 81st Street.

Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded in Edwardsville.  Also, there was at least a foot of water over Illinois Route 143 near intersection with Interstate 70.  Several roads in Collinsville were flooded with a couple of vehicles driven into the flood waters.  A couple of people had to be rescued from their stranded cars.  No injuries were reported.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Missouri Avenue in East St. Louis.  Also, the east bound lanes of Interstates 70/55/64 were flooded so the interstate had to be closed for a time.  In Lebanon, U.S. Highway 50 near intersection with Illinois Route 4 was closed due to high water.
Up to three inches fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Illinois Route 127 north of Carlyle and U.S. Highway 50 near Huey.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including U.S. Highway 51 just north of Sandoval and Red Stripe Road about a mile and a half southeast of Sandoval.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a bradford pear tree as well as several large limbs from another tree.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree at the intersection of Highway W and Highway PP.  The tree was blocking the intersection.

Up to three inches of rain fell in a two hour period causing flash flooding.  The main area of flooding was the I-55/I-70/I-64 merger in East St. Louis.  A van was stuck in six feet of water on the northbound lanes of I-55 near the I-64 split.  Three women were in the van.  A tow truck  was used to pull the vehicle from the flood waters.  There is construction in the area where the flooding happened which helped to aggravate the flooding situation.  Also an underpass in East St. Louis was flooded.  One driver drove into the flood waters and became stranded.  No injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree limb.  It fell onto a car in Tower Grove causing minor damage.

Thunderstorms remained stationary over eastern Madison County for several hours.  Up to 7 inches of rain fell during this time.  There were numerous reports of flash flooding.  The most serious flash flooding was at the interchange of Interstate 55 and Illinois Route 140 in Hamel.  The interstate was flooded at the underpass, especially the north bound lanes.  Several feet of water was in this location with several cars stuck in the flood waters. Traffic had to be diverted off the highway for a time until the flood waters went down.  Also, in Marine 6.80 inches of rain fell.  Numerous roads in town were flooded as well as Illinois Route 143 and Illinois Route 4.  Illinois Route 143 was flooded west of Marine because the heavy rainfall caused the lake on the northwest side of town to overflow and spill into a nearby creek, which rose and flooded Route 143.
Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads in the Farina area were flooded.

Up to 4 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including the intersection of Illinois Route 37 and Cartter Road.  Also, there was water over Route 161 extension just west of intersection with Buchanan Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a 6 inch diameter tree.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a couple of power lines.  One was laying across the road.
Thunderstorm winds blew over a large tree. It landed on an unoccupied car causing major damage.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a couple of large trees and a few power lines.
Thunderstorm winds snapped off a three foot diameter tree at its base along Bluff Road north of Valmeyer.
Thunderstorm winds blew over a tree in House Springs.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous tree limbs and a couple of Bradford pear trees near Highway K and Winding Woods Drive.  Also, a couple of fences sustained minor damage.

Thunderstorms winds caused a wide swath of wind damage across St. Peters.  There were several large trees blown down as well as numerous large tree limbs.  Also, several power lines were blown down.  One large tree fell onto a house causing major damage.  Another large tree fell onto the house causing minor damage.  No injuries were reported.

A levee broke on the Mississippi River side of St. Charles County, near river mile 200.  A mandatory evacuation of West Alton east of U.S. Highway 67 was put into affect.  The water from the levee break flooded 12 homes and 6 businesses.  No injuries were reported.
One inch hail fell in Hematite.

Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads within Meramec State Park were closed due to flash flooding.  Also, several roads in the New Haven and Washington areas were closed due to flash flooding.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs around town.  Also, a large tree was blown over onto a home causing moderate roof damage.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several tree limbs and power lines.  Also, a few large trees were snapped off.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous tree limbs and power lines in Bismarck, Park Hills and Bonne Terre.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree onto Highway 49 just north of Annapolis.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree across U.S. Highway 67 a couple of miles south of Cherokee Pass.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees and power lines in New Haven.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a tree across a road in Villa Ridge.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees and power lines in the Maryland Heights and Bridgeton.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees and power lines as well as numerous tree limbs in Greenville and Smithboro.
St. Louis County reported one death and 21 heat related injuries from 8/27 - 8/31.
St. Louis County reported four heat related injuries.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree in Silex.
Thunderstorm winds blew off shingles on several homes in Eureka and blew down a large tree limb in Maplewood.  The tree limb caused minor damage to a car.
Thunderstorm winds snapped several 10 to 12 inch diameter trees near Cuivre River State Park.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor roof damage to several homes on the south side of the  city.  Also, several trees were either uprooted or snapped off.

A tornado touchdown on Interstate 64, about 4.4 miles southwest of New Minden, blowing a tractor trailer off the interstate and causing minor injuries to the driver.  The tornado then began moving northeast towards New Minden.  The worst damage was about 2 miles west southwest of New Minden, where a small farm sustained a direct hit.  The outbuildings and barns sustained varying degrees of damage, but the homestead was totally destroyed with only the foundation remaining.  The damage at the homestead was rated EF4, and two fatalities occurred at this location.  Also, a large full size van was rolled over.  Less than a quarter of a mile east of the house, a single wide mobile home was destroyed.  There were 4 people at this location, three of them sought shelter in the creek bed just east of the mobile home while one went back to mobile home to retrieve something.  This person rode out the tornado in the bathtub, but was thrown about 50 feet into a field.  One of his ankles was broken.  He was treated and released from a local hospital.  The tornado then continued to race northeast, hitting the far north side of New Minden north of Illinois Route 177, and producing significant damage to St. Johns Lutheran Church and to several homes just northwest of the church.  Damage to two of the homes was rated EF3.  The tornado continued northeast, producing sporadic damage to just north of Hoyleton. A farm 2 miles west-northwest of Hoyleton sustained significant damage, as did a newly constructed home 2 miles north of Hoyleton.  Damage at these two locations were rated EF2.  The tornado then veered a bit northwest and dissipated.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 10.59 miles with a max path width of 200 yards. The tornado was rated EF4 with max wind speeds of at least 166 MPH.  There were two fatalities and 2 minor injuries.

As the EF4 tornado dissipated, another tornado formed one mile to the east on Sycamore Road just west of intersection with Peach Tree Road.  At this location, a barn had several of its walls collapsed on the south side of Sycamore Road.  The tornado then travelled to the northeast.  It crossed Peach Tree Road and destroyed a barn about four tenths of a mile north of Sycamore Road.  It continued to the northeast causing sporadic tree damage.  The most widespread damage occurred near the Flying M Ranch Golf Course, about 3 miles southwest of the city limits of Centralia, Illinois.  In this area the tornado lifted some panels off of a barn roof on Kuhn Road and caused significant roof damage to a house on County Highway 18 just south of Klub House Lane.  The damage to the house was rated EF1.  Just northeast of the house, the golf course club house sustained considerable roof damage and several windows were blown out.  The tornado continued to the northeast crossing from Washington County into far southeastern Clinton County, about a third of a mile west of Wilkin Road.  The path length of the tornado in Washington County was 3.58 miles with a max path width of 100 yards.  The damage for this segment was estimated to be EF1 with max wind speeds of 95 to 100 MPH.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 4.76 miles with a max path width of 100 yards and a maximum damage rating of EF1.

The tornado continued to the northeast crossing from Washington County into far southeastern Clinton County, about a third of a mile west of Wilkin Road.  It travelled to the northeast causing only tree damage before lifting and dissipating only three quarters of a mile west of a large mobile home park in Wamac.  The path length of the tornado in Clinton County was 1.18 miles with a max path width of 20 yards.  The damage for this segment was estimated to be EF0.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 4.76 miles with a max path width of 100 yards and a maximum damage rating of EF1.

Despite photographic evidence of a large tornado northwest of Litchfield, only minor damage to power poles and one barn was observed.  The tornado initially touched down in Macoupin County on Litchfield Road about 1.3 miles west of the Macoupin/Montgomery county line.  It travelled to the northeast only causing minor tree damage rated EF0 in Macoupin County.  It then crossed the Macoupin/Montgomery county line about four tenths of a mile south of North 18th Avenue.  Most of the area where the tornado occurred was bare farm fields which did not have any damage indicators.  The path length of the tornado in Macoupin County was 2.11 miles with a max path width of 20 yards.  The damage for this segment was estimated to be EF0.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 3.98 miles with a max path width of 50 yards and a maximum damage rating of EF0.

Despite photographic evidence of a large tornado northwest of Litchfield, only minor damage to power poles and one barn was observed.  The tornado crossed the Macoupin/Montgomery county line into Montgomery County about four tenths of a mile south of North 18th Avenue.  The tornado caused some minor tree damage on Barnett Trail.  It continued to the northeast causing moderate roof damage to a barn on the south side of Illinois Route 108, just west of intersection with Pipeline Road before lifting and dissipating.  Most of the area where the tornado occurred was bare farm fields which did not have any damage indicators.  The path length of the tornado in Montgomery County was 1.87 miles with a max path width of 50 yards.  The damage for this segment was estimated to be EF0.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 3.98 miles with a max path width of 50 yards and a maximum damage rating of EF0.

A tornado touched down on Jamestown Road about seven tenths of a mile south of the intersection with Low Bridge Road and moved east northeast about four tenths of a mile before dissipating.  It destroyed a garage, removed shingles from a house, destroyed a pole barn and snapped a number of large trees.  This tornado was photographed by numerous people.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 0.37 miles with a max path width of 50 yards. The tornado was rated EF1 with max wind speed of 100 MPH.

A strong tornado developed between U.S. Highway 40 and Interstate 70 about 1.4 miles east of Brownstown on County Road 1750E.  The tornado destroyed a barn, depositing the debris downstream into the adjacent open field.  The tornado continued northeast across U.S. Highway 40 damaging a few outbuildings and silos on a farmstead.  The tornado strengthened and grew in size as it moved just to the west of St. Elmo.  Here it caused significant damage to three homes and severe damage/complete destruction to numerous outbuildings.  Two of the houses were moved from their foundations. This damage was rated EF-2.  The tornado continued northeast toward the St. Elmo Golf Club, causing significant damage to trees and destroying a garage and two outbuildings at a residence located on St. Elmo Country Club Road.  The tornado continued northeast crossing Illinois Route 128 into Effingham County (WFO ILX���s county warning area).  The path length of the tornado in Fayette County was 8.5 miles with a max path width of 200 yards.  The damage for this segment was estimated to be EF2 with max wind speeds of 120 MPH.  Overall, the entire tornado path length was 11.4 miles with a max path width of 200 yards and a maximum damage rating of EF2.
Thunderstorm winds caused moderate damage to several homes in Nokomis.  Also, several homes sustained minor siding damage.
Gradient wind gust of 53 MPH at Jefferson City Memorial Airport at 1110 am.  Several power lines and trees were blown down by the gradient winds.
Gradient wind gust of 62 mph at St. Charles Smartt Airport.  The gradient winds caused minor roof damage to Heritage Primary School in Wentzville. Also, the winds broke a window at the school.
Gradient wind gust of 59 mph at Spirit of St. Louis Airport.  The gradient winds blew 3 vehicles off of the road near intersection of I-270 and Highway 364.
Gradient wind gust of 59 mph at Lambert-St. Louis International Airport at 1245 pm.  Gradient winds blew down a large tree in Oakville.
Gradient wind gust of 60 mph at Quincy Regional-Baldwin Field.
Gradient winds blew down several large trees around Alton.  The winds gusted to 55 MPH at Alton-St. Louis Regional Airport at 1250 pm.

Thunderstorm winds blew a utility pole down in Alton. The pole fell onto an occupied car.  One passenger sustained minor injuries.  In Bethalto, several large tree limbs and a two foot diameter tree were blown down.
Thunderstorm winds blew off some siding on a few homes as well as some shingles in the Highland area. A few small trees were blown down in Highland.
Thunderstorm winds blew off some shingles on a few homes around Aviston.  One mile west of Breese, a shed was blown down.
Thunderstorm winds blew shingles and sheeting off of a home in Ramsey.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several power lines in Kinmundy.

The tornado developed over the north side of Martinsburg, Illinois. One home sustained minor roof and fascia damage and one window was damaged along the south side of the home.  A few large trees and several large branches were downed by the tornado.  The tornado then traveled east-northeast and sheared a path of large pine trees 30 to 40 feet tall half a mile north of Martinsburg along and west of County Road 11.  Many of the pine trees were snapped from near the base to half way up the trunk.  The width of this damage area was 80 yards.  The next damage was found approximately 300 yards south of the intersection of County Road 7 and 205th Avenue.  A one story residence home sustained minor fascia damage and a few pine trees were snapped at the bases.  The tornado then totally destroyed a medium size machine shed on the south side of Watsons Cemetery east of the intersection. Several tomb stones were damaged.  Approximately 300 yards east of the cemetery another farmstead sustained damage.  Two empty medium size grain bins were destroyed while another machine shed was destroyed.  Damage was found again at another farmstead located 1 mile west of Detroit, Illinois.  The east side of a two story farm house was moved off its foundation by 5 inches while part of the east side of the roof was tossed to the east.  The upper half of a large barn was removed and tossed to the east. One old machine shed was completely destroyed while two canvas hoop sheds were completely destroyed.  Debris from the machine sheds were tossed a quarter of a mile to the east.  The tornado crossed Illinois Route 106 about a mile west of Detroit and damaged several large trees.  The tornado then directly hit a hog building which was supported by steel I-beams.  The southern part of the structure was pushed to the north and northeast.  Debris from the roof of this structure was tossed over half a mile to the northeast.  The damage width over this area was 80 yards wide.  Damage to this structure was rated EF-2. The tornado continued to the northeast destroying a shed before lifting and dissipating about a mile north northeast of Detroit. Several people were in the area of the shed working on repairing fencing.  One man sustained a minor shoulder injury and was taken to the hospital. The maximum intensity was EF2 with a maximum wind speed of 120 mph. The total path length was 12.09 miles with a maximum width 80 yards.

The tornado touched down 4 miles south southeast of Nokomis at the intersection of E 25th Road and Mt. Zion Trail. In this location it took a large section of shingles off of a garage roof and twisted the entire structure slightly off its foundation.  A little further to the northeast it took a large section of roof off of a barn. Some of the metal panels from the roof were thrown about half a mile to the northeast of the structure.  Just northeast of the barn, a double trussed metal transmission tower was blown down. Damage in this area was rated EF1.  The tornado continued to the northeast. Just north of the intersection of Oconee Avenue and E 28th Road, a two foot diameter oak tree was uprooted. Also, in this location there was a 50 yard wide path of major tree damage.  Several trees were uprooted on the west side of Litz Road, about six tenths of a mile north of the intersection of Litz Road and CR 2050N.  From there the tornado continued to the northeast and crossed into Shelby County (WFO Lincoln���s county warning area), about a third of a mile south of the intersection of E 30th Road and N 22nd Avenue. For Montgomery County portion of the tornado, the maximum intensity was EF1 with a max wind speed of 100 mph. The path length of this segment was 6.3 miles and a max width of 50 yards. Overall the maximum intensity was EF2 (in Shelby County about 3.5 miles north northwest of Tower Hill).  The total path length was 22.2 miles with a max path width of 200 yards.

The tornado developed 2.8 miles northwest of Brownstown or 0.3 miles north of the intersection of County Roads 1900N and 1375E. One large old tree was down while several large branches along a row of trees were snapped two thirds up the trunk. The damage path was approximately 40 yards wide and damage intensity was rated EF0. Two witnesses observed the tornado near the intersection of County Roads 2000N and 1450E. The tornado was rain wrapped and skipped over this area. One large machine shed was damaged about 150 yards southwest of this intersection while the southern part of another barn southeast of the intersection was severely damaged. Debris from both structures were tossed about one third mile to the northeast. At the intersection of 2100N and 1600E three tall wooden transmission line poles were snapped two thirds up the pole at this intersection.  Approximately 50 yards to the southeast of this intersection a medium size machine shed was severely damaged with the east and south sides of the shed shredded and tossed one third mile to the northeast. The tornado continued northeast and destroyed a large machine shed housing farm equipment. The tornado totally shredded the metal panels and tossed them over one third mile to the north. A medium size machine shed approximately one half mile to the northeast of the large machine shed lost a few metal roof panels.  The tornado lifted and dissipated about 5.5 miles north northeast of Brownstown. The maximum intensity was EF1 with a maximum wind speed of 105 mph. The total path length was 4.8 miles with a maximum width 50 yards.

The tornado touched down about 3.4 miles northeast of Highland, in Madison County, on Trestle Road causing window, roof and tree damage to a home, and then totally destroyed a large commercial metal storage building just northeast of the home.  The tornado then crossed the county line into Bond County. For the Madison County portion of the tornado, the maximum intensity was EF1 with a path length of 1.06 miles and a max path width of 50 yards. Overall, the maximum intensity for the entire tornado was EF1 with a maximum wind speed of 105 mph. The total path length was 12.31 miles with a maximum width 50 yards.

After crossing from Madison County into Bond County, the tornado continued to produce intermittent tree damage as it headed northeast and crossed Illinois Route 143 and then totally destroyed a farm outbuilding along Pokey Road. Another farmstead was struck northeast of the farm outbuilding, where the tornado totally destroyed a pole barn and produced extensive damage to a home from a falling oak tree. The tornado continued to produce damage to trees and outbuildings as it moved northeast with roof and siding damage also occurring to a home on Millersburg Road. It lifted and dissipated just southwest of the intersection of Airport Avenue and Dudleyville Road, three miles south of Greenville. For the Bond County portion of the tornado, the maximum intensity was EF1 with a path length of 11.25 miles and a max path width of 50 yards. Overall, the maximum intensity for the entire tornado was EF1 with a maximum wind speed of 105 mph. The total path length was 12.31 miles with a maximum width 50 yards.
A 58 mph non-thunderstorm wind gust was recorded at Columbia Regional Airport.
Gradient winds blew a mini greenhouse over in Lyon. Also, several houses in Lyon and Pacific had some shingles blown off. In Pacific, several trees and signs were blown down.
A 67 mph non-thunderstorm wind gust was recorded at Smartt Field.  The winds blew off some shingles on a few homes northeast of Marthasville.
Gradient winds blew over a semi on U.S. Highway 61 near Highway WW. No injuries reported.
Gradient winds blew over several trees in the Belleview area.  One tree blocked County Road 20 briefly.
A 62 mph gradient wind gust was recorded at Lambert-St. Louis International Airport. Also, Spirit of St. Louis Airport recorded a gradient wind gust of 58 mph.
A 60 mph non-thunderstorm wind gust was recorded at Centralia Municipal Airport.
A 59 mph non-thunderstorm wind gust was recorded at Scott AFB.
A gradient wind gust of 63 mph was recorded at Alton-St. Louis Regional Airport. The gradient winds blew down several trees in Collinsville, some of which blocked roadways.
Two semi trucks were blown off of I-55 near mile marker 41 in far southeast Macoupin County by gradient winds.  No injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees around town.
As a severe storm moved through Callaway county, a wide swath of large hail fell from just west of Fulton to Williamsburg.  In Calwood, one inch hail caused siding damage to several homes.
A second severe storm quickly followed on the heals of the previous storm and dumped another swath of large hail, mainly in Fulton.
A large swath of hail fell across Madison County from Granite City to the Glen Carbon area.
Up to 4 inches of rain fell in a very short amount of time causing flash flooding.  South Fillmore Avenue was flooded near East Monroe.  In Maryland Heights, Fee Fee creek rose above its flood stage.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees and numerous power lines.

A weak tornado touched down just west of Interstate 170 in the backyard of a residence on Stoneleigh Towers St. at 5:19 a.m. CDT, uprooting several large mature hardwood trees and topping a large pine tree.  It crossed Interstate 170 and caused minor damage to trees and roofs in an apartment complex and adjacent office building along Old Towne Dr.  The tornado then caused more significant tree damage east along Rowland Drive toward N. McKnight Road.  A few houses were hit by trees causing significant damage. The tornado grew to its largest width, about 100 yards, while crossing N. McKnight Road.  It is here that the most concentrated damage occurred with many houses loosing siding, roofing and having windows blown out by debris.  Many large trees were uprooted and one tree adjacent to the Ruth Park Golf Club experienced significant twisting of the branches. The tornado continued east causing similar damage along Charters Ave.  The tornado then weakened and dissipated at 5:21 a.m. after uprooting several large trees in the Ruth Park Golf Club.  A total of 100 buildings were damaged by the tornado and damaging straight line thunderstorm winds, 20 had significant damage, and several cars were destroyed by falling trees or large limbs. Overall, the maximum intensity was EF1 with a total path length of 0.63 miles.  The max path width was 100 yards.

Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees as well as numerous tree limbs and power lines.  One tree fell onto a house causing moderate damage.  Another tree fell onto an unoccupied car crushing it.  A two and a half foot diameter pine tree was snapped.

Thunderstorm winds uprooted one large tree and caused minor damage to a nearby home.  Also, further northeast a lean-to was destroyed with the debris thrown into a nearby field, power lines and a pickup truck.
Baseball sized hail produced holes in siding on several homes.  Also, the hail damaged vinyl window sills and gutters.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees in St. Thomas.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several 18 to 20 inch diameter trees in Meta.
Thunderstorm winds blew over a truck pulling a trailer about two miles west of Fairview Heights.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a tree across a road two miles south of St. Jacob.
Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  U.S. Highway 50 had a foot of water flowing over it about a mile west of Tipton.
Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were closed due to water over the roadways in the south half of Boone County.

Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Elmont Road at the intersection with Deer Path was washed out by the flooding rains. Several roads in the area were closed due to flooding.
Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Several roads were flooded including Highway 185 between Pea Ridge and Caseyville.

Up to four inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding. Numerous roads were flooded including the intersection of Highway 1 and Beaver Creek Road, about two miles east of Addieville.  Also, County Road 6 east of Venedy had water flowing over it.
Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous roads were flooded including several around the Waterloo area.
Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.  Numerous low water crossings were flooded.

Thunderstorm winds destroyed 3 large barns on a farm at the intersection of Meridian Road and County Road 1500N. It was on the west side of Meridian Road in Clinton County. Meridian Road is the county line between Clinton County and Marion County.  Six out of 600 cows died in one of the barns.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree limb in New Bloomfield.  A large spruce tree was blown down in Fulton.  Also, several homes sustained minor shingle damage.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree in Owensville.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees.  A couple of the trees knocked down power lines causing power outages.

Thunderstorm winds caused widespread damage in Lincoln County.  In Troy, winds lifted the roof off of an attached garage.  The garage door was open at the time the winds blew through.  Also, several trees and fences were blown down around town.  South of Troy on Highway U, several power lines were blown down onto the roadway.  In Elsberry, some shingles were blown off of several homes.
Thunderstorm winds blew over an anchored aluminum carport and destroyed it.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree onto Route Y near intersection with County Road 379.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several power lines north of Warrenton near the Warren/Lincoln county line.
Thunderstorm winds broke several store windows in downtown Troy. Also, numerous tree limbs were blown down around town.

Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees.  One tree in Ladue fell onto an unoccupied car destroying it.  In Pagedale, a large tree fell onto a house causing moderate damage.  Also, one occupant sustained minor injuries.

Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees on the north side of St. Louis.  One tree fell onto two homes in the 4200 block of Darby causing moderate damage.  Just northeast of this area, an industrial building had a wall and part of its roof blown down.  No injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree and numerous large tree limbs just east of Dow.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees.  Also, an old barn was blown down.
Thunderstorm winds caused moderate damage to a cattle shed.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs 5 miles northeast of Granville and blew one tree over onto power lines about 5 miles north of Paris.
Large swath of one inch hail fell across most of Columbia as storm moved east through town.
Several 8 to 10 inch diameter trees were blown down in Dow.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several power lines around Nashville.

Thunderstorm winds caused widespread wind damage across the northern half of Knox County.  In Hurdland, several trees were blown down or uprooted.  In Edina, numerous trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.  Several trees in Edina caused minor to moderate roof damage to a couple of homes.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees as well as numerous tree limbs in Lewistown.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous large tree limbs and some windows on businesses on the east side of Quincy.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees and numerous tree limbs around Columbia.  Also, two miles south of Ashland part of the roof of a barn was blown off.
Several large trees were blown over onto Illinois Route 16.

Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees and numerous tree limbs.  Five miles west of Union on Highway AJ, three power poles were snapped.  In Union, a man was briefly trapped in his car by fallen trees. He only sustained minor injuries.

Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees on Highway T near Labadie.  In Catawissa, several trees and numerous tree limbs were blown down.  One tree caused moderate damage to a house and an unoccupied car.
Thunderstorm winds snapped several 8 inch diameter trees in Cedar Hill.
A tornado briefly touched down twice in an open field northeast of Owensville, north of Highway 28.  No damage was reported with it.

The tornado touched down on Cedar Grove Court causing minor roof damage to two buildings in the Cedar Grove Apartment complex.  Some shingles were removed and small pieces of the roofing panel were also removed at this apartment complex.  Also, several medium size trees were snapped off as well as numerous tree limbs.  The tornado continued to the east northeast crossing Harvester Road and then crossed Highway 94 at the junction with Jungermann Road.  On the northeast side of the intersection, a business sustained moderate damage.  Many cinder blocks on the upper front side fell to the ground next to the entrance.  Two overhangs were also destroyed on the building.  Further to the east northeast, two single story homes on Queens Brooke Blvd. between Jungermann Road and Harvester Road sustained minor roof damage.  Twenty percent of the shingles were removed from each of these homes.  A wooden fence on the back side of these residences was also knocked down.  Small trees less than 30 feet tall and less than 8 inches in diameter were snapped at the base on McClay Village Drive, just south of McClay Road.  Two homes on McClay Gardens Drive each sustained damage to the fascia and roof.  A one story residence on McClay Road between Harvester Road and Hackmann Road lost 40 percent of its roofing material.  A few small panels were also uplifted on the south side of this home.  On the east side of the home, a forty foot pine tree with a diameter of 12 inches was snapped half way up and was tossed 20 yards towards the northeast into an open field.  Additional minor tree damage was located on Woodbriar Lane northeast of McClay Road.  The tornado lifted and dissipated at the intersection of Hackmann Road and Woodbriar Lane.  Overall, the tornado was rated EF0.  It was on the ground for 2.67 miles with a max path width of 20 yards.

The tornado touched down approximately 50 yards north of the intersection of Earth City Express Way and St. Charles Rock Road.  A stop sign and minor tree damage occurred at this location.  Video from a storm chaser showed the tornado then travelled over Interstate 370 east of the Earth City Express Way/I-370 interchange, lofting debris.  The tornado was also observed and videotaped while passing west and northwest of the Mills Outlet Mall.  Tree branch damage was found on Garner Lane northwest of the mall and near the intersection of Teson Road and Aubuchon Road.  The tornado paralleled  Aubuchon Road and then hit two machine sheds.  About 90 percent of the panels from one machine shed were removed while 40 percent of the panels were removed from the second machine shed.  The tornadic damage was 40 yards wide at this location.  The tornado continued to move northeast and travelled over Charbonier Road and caused more minor tree damage just north of the road.  The tornado then lifted and dissipated.  Overall, the tornado was rated EF0. It was on the ground for 4.22 miles with a max path width of 40 yards.

A tornado touched down on the north end of Fults, just north of Ivy Road, southwest of where the train tracks cross Ivy Road.  In this location the corn crop was snapped off.  The tornado continued to the northeast snapping off half of a large maple tree.  The tree fell onto a house causing moderate damage.  Also, several smaller trees in the area were damaged.
